item.title: U-Boot firmware flaws, EU CSAM scanning vote, and healthcare cyberattacks
item.content:encoded:
New U-Boot flaws could enable stealthy firmware attacks — Should Read

Six vulnerabilities in the widely used U-Boot bootloader could let attackers crash devices or run malicious code before the operating system loads, enabling stealthy and persistent firmware compromise. Patches are upstream, but affected devices remain at risk until hardware vendors ship firmware updates, and older unsupported products may never be fixed.

  • Binarly disclosed six vulnerabilities in U-Boot's FIT signature verification code that range in impact from denial of service to arbitrary code execution during verification of an untrusted image.
  • U-Boot is widely used in embedded Linux devices, including enterprise servers' Baseboard Management Controllers, networking equipment, industrial systems, IoT devices, and other appliances.
  • Two of the flaws can potentially lead to arbitrary code execution during firmware verification, while the remaining four can be exploited to crash vulnerable devices.
  • Most of the vulnerable code has existed since U-Boot version 2013.07, potentially affecting more than 50 stable releases and downstream vendor firmware forks.
  • Patches for all six issues have been accepted upstream, but hardware manufacturers must incorporate the fixes into their own firmware updates before customers receive them.

Europe revives law allowing big tech to scan for CSAM — Should Read

The European Parliament revived a legal exemption allowing major tech companies like Google, Microsoft and Meta to voluntarily scan users’ messages for child sexual abuse material until 2028. Critics say the procedural vote undermined privacy protections and foreshadows a larger fight over “Chat Control 2.0,” which could mandate scanning even in encrypted services.

  • The European Parliament voted to revive a 2021 rule allowing big tech companies to voluntarily scan users’ messages for child sexual abuse material.
  • The revived rule gives companies such as Google, Microsoft, and Meta legal cover to continue CSAM scanning until 2028.
  • The vote used an unusual procedure requiring an absolute majority to kill the provision, meaning absent lawmakers were effectively counted in favor of the measure.
  • Critics said the procedural move was disturbing because Parliament had rejected the same measure three months earlier under normal circumstances.
  • A larger dispute continues over a proposed permanent framework called Chat Control 2.0, which could force service providers to scan conversations and hosted content, including end-to-end encrypted communications.

Cybercriminals Flock to Healthcare Businesses as Attacks Surge — Optional

Cybercriminals are increasingly targeting healthcare service providers and related businesses, with attacks more than doubling in the first half of 2026, while hospitals continue to face impersonation, social engineering, legacy device, staffing, and third-party security challenges.

  • Cyberattacks against hospitals and clinics grew modestly in the first half of 2026.
  • Attacks on service providers and other healthcare businesses more than doubled in the first half of 2026.
  • Hospitals are seeing more impersonation and social engineering-driven attacks, according to Errol Weiss, chief security officer at Health-ISAC.
  • Errol Weiss said hospitals continue to face challenges finding and patching legacy devices.
  • Errol Weiss said hospital CISOs identify their top challenge as having enough resources to adequately protect hospital networks, including budget for experienced cybersecurity talent and needed technology.

NIST Elevated DNS Security. Censys Active DNS Connects Names to Live Internet Infrastructure. — Optional

Censys is promoting Active DNS as a way to turn DNS records into actionable security evidence by linking domains to live hosts, services, certificates, vulnerabilities, and historical infrastructure changes. The pitch is framed around NIST’s stronger emphasis on DNS security in SP 800-81r3 and CSF 2.0 alignment.

  • NIST SP 800-81r3 is mapped to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, giving DNS security a clearer place in how organizations structure risk, governance, and security operations.
  • Censys Active DNS actively resolves names by querying authoritative infrastructure and connects those results to the broader Censys Internet Map.
  • Censys Active DNS lets security teams examine current and historical A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, SOA, and TXT records, including when records were first and last seen by Censys.
  • Censys connects domain indicators to resolved hosts, open ports, running services, certificates, CVEs, host reputation, threat context, HTTP content, and screenshots.
  • The article says Censys Active DNS can support exposure management, threat hunting, detection engineering, incident response, and SOC triage for teams aligning to CSF 2.0.
